newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish markets confident of timely EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Spanish markets confident of timely EMU start.

text.p: Despite concern over possible delays to European economic and monetary union (EMU), Spanish markets are firm, unable to see any scenario but steady convergence toward a single European currency in 1999.
EMU jitters so far have been mainly a matter of words, and markets are proving resilient to doubts cast by the new French government and by the Bonn-Bundesbank gold revaluation row.
Although an increase in volatility and market corrections are always on the cards, dealers and analysts in Spain remain very bullish.

"People in Spain and Italy realized that if they were almost sure to enter (EMU) before the French vote, afterwards their entrance is even more sure," said Carlos de La Pena at AB Asesores, one of Spain's biggest non-bank brokers, in Madrid.

At 1130 GMT, the long bond future was trading 28 basis points lower at 115.62, just one point short of its record high of 116.64. The 10-year spread over Bunds was at 74 basis points, not far from its record low of 64 basis points on May 21.
"It seems to me volatility (of options on bond future) should be higher. But it's still close to a record low. That's because the market is really bullish," said a trader in Madrid.
He said volatility on 10-year September bond futures was trading at around 6.80/7.00 percent.
"EMU expectations remain positive and especially after the vote in France a broader EMU with Spain and Italy is more likely," said Francesco Giordano, economist at CSFB in London.
CSFB calculates a 35 percent probability of a timely EMU, 45 percent for a short delay of about nine months and 20 percent for a longer delay of the single currency's start.
In recent years, the political commitment behind a European single currency has been so high that markets do not believe European countries would suddenly give up, analysts said.
"They can't simply say to their voters that all the efforts, in term of fiscal tightness and higher taxes, have been in vain," said Marco Pianelli, economist at Nomura in London.
"Either there's a timely euro or there's no euro at all," he added.
The EU Amsterdam summit on June 16 and 17, when European heads of state are expected to give their final approval of the stability pact, is seen as key.
"I guess France will also end up giving its approval to the Stability pact,'' Giordano said. -- Madrid Newsroom + 341 585 8340
